newsitem.title: USA: Shell Oil net jumps helped by oil production.
newsitem.headline: Shell Oil net jumps helped by oil production.

text.p: Shell Oil Co Tuesday reported sharply higher fourth quarter and annual earnings citing increased oil production in the Gulf of Mexico and China.

Significantly higher oil and natural gas prices also helped in the quarter, when refining and marketing margins were essentially unchanged despite deteriorating conditions in the U.S. West Coast Market.

The Royal Dutch/Shell Group subsidiary reported a record net income for 1996 of $2.02 billion, an increase of $501 million over the comparable 1995 period and highest annual net income in the company's 84-year history.
Excluding special items in both periods, adjusted net income was up 32 percent for the year and 88 percent for the fourth quarter, Shell said.
"For 1996, we achieved a 10.5 percent return on investment, the highest level in the last 15 years," President Phillip Carroll said.
Capital expenditures for 1996 totaled $3.41 billion, an increase of $457 million over 1995, primarily due to a higher level of spending in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico.
Shell said the latest quarter benefited from significantly higher crude oil and natural gas prices.

Domestic crude prices averaged $20.80 per barrel, up $6.21 over 1995, while total natural gas prices averaged $2.76 per thousand cubic feet, up $0.84. The quarter also benefited from increased domestic and international crude oil production.

Average U.S. production of crude oil increased in the 1996 quarter and full year over the comparable 1995 periods, as higher production, primarily in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico, more than offset natural declines elsewhere. International crude oil production also increased in both 1996 periods, due to increased liftings in China, Shell said.
It said natural gas production decreased slightly in the 1996 quarter from 1995, but for the full year increased 3 percent to 1.88 billion cubic feet a day, the highest level in the past 15 years.
Excluding special items, oil products income slipped $10 million in the quarter, but the 1996 total was up $95 million from 1995.

Shell said the quarterly decline reflected increased operating expenses. Margins were essentially unchanged despite West Coast retail marketing conditions deteriorating. Full-year results benefited from higher refined product margins, which were weak industry-wide in 1995.

Overall sales volumes of refined products increased in the fourth quarter and the full-year 1996. Sales of light oils increased 8 percent and 7 percent in the 1996 periods over 1995, while sales of branded automotive gasolines increased by about 1 percent when compared to the 1995 periods.

Chemical margins declined in the fourth quarter due to lower selling prices and higher feedstock costs across most product lines. For the year, results declined significantly due to lower margins across most product lines, partially offset by increased sales volumes of primary chemicals.
